The discussion of *al-zilzāl* has already preceded in the commentary on Surat al-Ḥajj.

The verb *zulzilat* is in the passive form (*ṣīghat al-nā'ib 'an al-fā'il*) because its agent is known, and he is God Most High.

*Zilzālahā* is in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ūl muṭlaq*), emphasizing its verb, to indicate the awfulness of that earthquake. The meaning is: "when the earth is shaken with a shaking."

*Zilzālahā* is annexed to the pronoun of *al-arḍ* (the earth) to convey that the shaking is firmly established in it and recurs, so that it becomes, as it were, known by its attribution to it because of its frequent connection with it. This is like the verse of al-Nābigha:

*Asā'iltī safāhatahā wa jahlan 'alā al-hijrāni ukhtu banī Shihāb*
"You, my questioner, ask about its foolishness and ignorance, [while] on the matter of separation, the sister of the Banū Shihāb [is the one who knows it]."

That is, "its foolishness," meaning that foolishness is characteristic of it, i.e., it is known for it. Also like the verse of Abū Khālid al-Qanānī:

*Wallāhu asmāka sumyan mubārakan ātharaka Allāhu bihi īthārakā*
"God named you with a blessed name, with which God chose you with preference."

He means a preference by which you became known and singled out.

In the books of biography (*kutub al-sīra*), there is a saying of Khaṭr ibn Mālik the soothsayer, mentioning his demon when he was stoned: *Balbalahu balbālu*, meaning: "a shaking that is firmly established in him."

The repetition of the word *al-arḍ* in His saying ﴿and the earth brought forth its burdens﴾ is an explicit mention in place of a pronoun, for the purpose of intensifying the awe.

*Al-athqāl* is the plural of *thiql* (with a kasra on the *thā'* and a sukūn on the *qāf*), which is heavy goods, and it is also applied to precious goods.

The bringing forth by the earth of its burdens results from the splitting of its surface, so it casts out what is in it of minerals, waters, and rocks. That is from the repeated eruptions arising from the turmoil within its layers and the reversal of their upper parts to become lower and vice versa.

The definiteness of *al-insān* ("the human being") is the definiteness of the genus (*ta'rīf al-jins*), which conveys comprehensiveness (*istighrāq*). That is: "And the people said, 'What is wrong with it?'" meaning the people who are alive, so they were terrified, and some said to others, or each one said to himself, so that in this the coward and the brave, the careless and the wise, are equal, because it is a shaking that exceeds the limit that the patient endures.

The statement *mā lahā* ("what is wrong with it") is a question about the thing that has become established for the earth and attached to it, since the *lām* conveys specification (*ikhtiṣāṣ*). That is: "What belongs to the earth in this shaking?" Or: "What is it [the earth] that it has been shaken with this shaking?" That is, "what will its outcome be?" The earth is treated as a purposeful agent whom people ask about the aim of its act, since its purpose from the act has not been made clear. Such a question usually comes accompanied by what relates to the stability stated in the predicate, as when one says: "What is with him, that he does such-and-such?" or "What is with him in doing such-and-such?" or "What is with him and so-and-so?" meaning, "with him." Therefore a supplied element must be assumed here: "What is it [the earth], that it was shaken?" or "What is it in this shaking?" or "What is it, and the bringing forth of its burdens?"

The clause ﴿On that day it will report its news﴾ and so on is the apodosis (*jawāb*) of *idhā* ("when"), with respect to what replaces it in His saying ﴿On that day the people will come forth﴾. So *yawma'idhin* is a substitute (*badal*) for *yawma'idhin tuḥaddithu akhbārahā*.

*Al-yawm* is applied to the daytime together with its night, so the shaking happens by day and is followed by events at night, along with the dimming and scattering of the stars. It may also be meant by *al-yawm* the absolute time.

*Tuḥaddithu akhbārahā* is the governing element (*al-'āmil*) for *yawma'idhin* and for the substitute. The estimated sense is: "On the day when the earth is shaken and brings forth its burdens, and people say, 'What is wrong with it, that it reports its news?'" and so on.

*Akhbāraha* is the second object of the verb *tuḥaddithu*, because it is among the verbs assimilated to *ẓanna* (to think), used to convey that the report gives knowledge. Its first object is omitted because it is evident, meaning: "it reports to the human being," since the purpose of the speech is its informing, for in it there is awe.

The pronoun in *tuḥaddithu* refers back to *al-arḍ*.

*Al-taḥdīth* in its real meaning is that a speech arises conveying a report about an event. It is reported in the Ḥadīth of al-Tirmidhī, from Abū Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited this verse ﴿On that day it will report its news﴾ and said: 'Do you know what its news is?' They said: 'God and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'Its news is that it will bear witness against every male and female servant of what they did upon its back. It will say: "He did on such-and-such a day such-and-such." That is its news.'" End of quotation.

*Akhbāruha* is in the plural because its indication of the number of speakers is multiple (*ta'addud dalālatihā 'alā 'adad al-qā'ilīn*), while *mā lahā* is a single report, and it is the one explained by His saying ﴿that your Lord has inspired it﴾.

[Page 493]

*Akhbāraha* is in the accusative by the removal of the governing preposition, which is the *bā'* of transitivity of the verb *tuḥaddithu*.

His saying ﴿that your Lord has inspired it﴾ may be connected to the verb *tuḥaddithu*, with the *bā'* indicating cause (*sababiyya*), meaning: "It reports its news because your Lord commanded it to report its news."

It may also be a substitute for *akhbāraha*, and the *bā'* is expressed in the substitute to emphasize the transitivity of the verb *tuḥaddithu* to it. In both cases its news is left general (*ujmilat*), and the preceding Ḥadīth explains it.

Inspiration (*al-waḥy*) is applied to the command of creation (*amr al-takwīn*), that is, He placed in it the causes of bringing forth its burdens, so it is as if He had confided to it a speech, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee: Take for yourselves houses in the mountains﴾ [al-Naḥl: 68], and the verses following.

The verb *awḥā* is transitive by the *lām* because *awḥā* is made to imply the meaning of *qāla* ("said"), like His saying: ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: Come willingly or unwillingly﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 11]. Otherwise, the proper construction of *awḥā* is with the preposition *ilā* ("to").

The implied saying is the saying of creation, as God says: ﴿Our command to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Naḥl: 40].

The reason that one turned from the verb *qāla lahā* to the verb *awḥā lahā* is that it is a report about creation, not about a verbal utterance.

His saying ﴿On that day the people will come forth in scattered groups﴾ is a substitute for the clause ﴿On that day it will report its news﴾, and the apodosis is the verb *yaṣduru al-nās* ("the people will come forth"), and His saying *yawma'idhin* is connected to it. It was placed before its complement for emphasis (*li'l-ihtimām*). This apodosis is the intended purpose of the speech, because the speech is directed toward establishing the gathering (*al-ḥashr*), reminding of it, and warning of its terrors, for when it occurs people will know that the earthquake was a warning of this gathering.

The literal meaning of *yaṣduru al-nās* is going out from the place where they gather. It is said: *ṣadara 'an al-makān* when one leaves it and goes out from it, *ṣudūran* and *ṣadaran* (with vowel-change). From this comes *al-ṣadr 'an al-mā'* ("departing from the water after the watering"). So the verb *yaṣduru* is applied here to the going out of people to the gathering in groups, or their dispersal from the place of gathering to their abodes in Paradise or Hell, by way of comparison with people departing from water after watering.

*Ashtāt* is the plural of *shatt* (with a fatha on the *shīn* and a shadda on the *tā'*), which is "scattered." The meaning is: they come forth scattered in groups, each toward a direction according to their deeds and what has been appointed for them of stations.

It is indicated that their dispersal is according to the proportion of each group in its deeds, from the ranks of goodness and the stations of evil, by His saying ﴿so that they may be shown their deeds﴾, meaning: they come forth for the purpose of receiving the recompense of the deeds they did in the worldly life, so it is said to each group: "Look at your deeds," or "Look at your end."

The verb *li-yurawū* is built in the passive form (to the substitute agent, *al-nā'ib*), because the intended meaning is their seeing their deeds, not specifying who shows them to them. The reciters have unanimously agreed on the *ḍamma* on the *yā'* (*taḥtiyya*).

So the seeing is used in the sense of visual seeing, and what is seen is the stations of recompense. It is also possible that the seeing is used in the sense of knowledge of the recompense of deeds, since deeds are not seen, but their recompense appears to their people.

[Page 495]

**﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.﴾**

This is a consequence (*tafri'*) of His saying ﴿that they may be shown their deeds﴾ [al-Zalzalah 99:6]. It is a consequence in the sense of a summary (*fadhlaka*), shifting to encouragement and warning after the completion of establishing the Resurrection and the recompense. The consequence implies that this occurs right after people depart in scattered groups.

*Al-mithqal* is that by which the weight of a thing is known, that by which weight is measured. It is like a balance (*mizan*) in its weight and meaning.

*Al-dharrah* is the small ant at the beginning of its life.

﴿An atom's weight﴾ is a figure of speech for the smallest of quantities. For believers this is evident. As for disbelievers, what is intended is the evil they did. As for their good deeds, they are as nothing, so they are not described as good in the sight of God, because doing good is conditional upon faith. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert plain, which the thirsty one takes for water, until when he comes to it he finds it to be nothing﴾ [al-Nur 24:39].

[Page 495 continued]
The phrase "whoever does" was repeated without relying on the conjunction, so that each sentence would be independently clear in its meaning, and so that each sentence would be devoted to its purpose of encouragement or warning. The importance of this requires explicitness and elaboration.

This verse is counted among the *jawami' al-kalim* (comprehensive utterances), and the Prophet ﷺ described it as "the unique comprehensive [verse]." In the *Muwatta'*: "The Prophet ﷺ said: Horses are for three [purposes]..." the hadith [continues]. He was asked about donkeys, and he said: "Nothing was revealed to me concerning them except this unique comprehensive verse: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.﴾"

Ibn Mas'ud narrated that he said: "This is the most decisive verse in the Qur'an." Al-Hasan said: "Sa'sa'ah ibn Najiyah, grandfather of al-Farazdaq, came to the Prophet ﷺ seeking to have the Prophet recite the Qur'an to him. He recited this verse to him, and Sa'sa'ah said: 'Enough for me, for the admonition has reached its end; I do not mind not hearing anything else of the Qur'an.'" Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "God sent down to Muhammad two verses that encompassed what is in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the scrolls: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.﴾"

Since the discourse was directed toward both encouragement and warning together, the aspect of encouragement was given precedence in the division, as an honoring of the people of good.

In *al-Kashshaf*: It is related that a Bedouin delayed "will see it" [in the order of the verse], so it was said to him: "You put first and postponed," and he said:

*"Take the belly of Harsha or its back, for both sides of Harsha are paths for them."*

This Bedouin overlooked the eloquence of the verse, which requires honoring the people of good.

Al-Wahidi narrated from Muqatil that this verse was revealed concerning two men who were in Medina. One of them did not mind minor sins and would commit them, and the other loved to give charity but found only a little, so he was ashamed to give it away. So the verse was revealed concerning both of them.

Because of this narration, a group said that the surah is Medinan. But even if this report is sound, it would not necessarily imply that the surah is Medinan, because when they recited a verse of the Qur'an as evidence, some of the listeners would suppose it had been revealed concerning that event, as we have explained in the Fifth Introduction.

**In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful**

**Surat al-'Adiyat**

It is named in the ancient Qayrawani, Tunisian, and Eastern codices of the Qur'an as "Surat al-'Adiyat" without a *waw*, and likewise in some tafsir works. So it is named after what is mentioned in it, without quoting its exact wording. In some books of tafsir it is named "Surat wal-'Adiyat," with the *waw*.

Scholars differed about it. Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir ibn Zayd, 'Ata', al-Hasan, and 'Ikrimah said: it is Meccan. Anas ibn Malik, Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah said: it is Medinan.

In the order of the revelation of surahs, according to Jabir ibn Zayd, it is counted as the fourteenth, on the basis that it is Meccan, revealed after Surat al-'Asr and before Surat al-Kawthar.

Its verses number eleven.

Al-Wahidi mentioned in *Asbab al-Nuzul*, from Muqatil and others, that "the Messenger of God ﷺ sent a expedition of horses to the Banu Kinanah, and appointed over them al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr al-Ansari. They were away for a month (*asheebat*, i.e., they went far into a wide land, *sahb*, which is the vast earth), and their good tidings were delayed. The hypocrites spread rumors and said: 'They have all been killed.' So God informed about them with His saying: ﴿By the racing ones, panting﴾ [al-'Adiyat 100:1] and the verses that follow, informing that their horses had done all that is in those verses."

This hadith, *al-Itqan* said, was narrated by al-Hakim and others. Ibn Kathir said: Abu Bakr al-Bazzar narrated here a very strange hadith, and he related a hadith close to what al-Wahidi related.

I say: the strangeness of a hadith does not contradict its acceptance, and it is narrated from reliable narrators. However, in its chain is Hafs ibn Jumay', who is weak. So the more probable view is that the surah is Medinan.

* * *

**Its purposes**

Condemnation of qualities that lead their possessors to loss in the Hereafter, which are qualities prevalent among the polytheists and hypocrites, and the aim is to warn the Muslims against them.

All of this is emphasized by beginning with an oath, and within the oath is included an honoring of the horses of the warriors or the mounts of the pilgrims.
